Power Electronics & Protection
SCR Triggering Methods: Forward Voltage, dv/dt, Temperature, Light and Gate Triggering with RC and UJT Firing Circuits

An SCR blocks until something pushes its middle junction into conduction, and there are five ways to do that. Only gate triggering gives you a controlled, repeatable firing instant, so most of what follows is about the gate and how to drive it.

Five turn on methods DC, AC and pulse gate drive RC and UJT firing Gate resistor calculator Fault finding flowchart

Overvoltage, a fast rising voltage, heat, light or a gate signal can all switch on an SCR. Here we compare SCR triggering methods and size a gate resistor.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn SCR triggering methods, why gate pulse triggering is the method used in real converters, and how to size the gate resistor with a worked example.
Quick Answer

What are SCR triggering methods and which one is used in practice?

SCR triggering methods are the ways to drive a forward biased SCR from its blocking state into conduction: forward voltage triggering, dv/dt triggering, temperature triggering, light triggering and gate triggering. In practice we use gate triggering, usually with short pulses through a pulse transformer or optocoupler. For example, a 12 V pulse through a 175 ohm resistor pushes 60 mA into a gate rated 30 mA IGT.

What Are SCR Triggering Methods?

SCR triggering methods are the ways we turn a forward biased silicon controlled rectifier from its blocking state into its conducting state. Five physical effects can do it, and gate triggering is the only one engineers use on purpose in a working circuit.

Key Facts
  • With anode positive, the middle junction J2 of the PNPN structure blocks current.
  • Forward voltage, dv/dt and temperature turn on are treated as faults.
  • Gate triggering can be DC, AC or pulse; pulse is preferred.
  • Once latched, the SCR stays on until anode current falls below IH.
Advertisement

How Does an SCR Turn On?

An SCR turns on when the current gains of its two internal transistors add up to one, at which point the device latches by positive feedback. Every one of the SCR triggering methods is just a different way of raising that gain.

Picture the PNPN structure as a PNP transistor and an NPN transistor connected so that the collector of each drives the base of the other. Our pages on silicon controlled rectifiers and transistor basics cover the structure in more detail.

Two transistor model of the SCR
IA = (α2 × IG + ICBO1 + ICBO2) / 1 minus (α1 + α2)
When α1 + α2 approaches 1, IA is limited only by the load
Do You Know?

General Electric introduced the SCR in 1957, and it quickly replaced mercury arc rectifiers in industrial drives.

What Are the Turn On Methods of SCR?

The five turn on methods of an SCR are forward voltage triggering, dv/dt triggering, temperature triggering, light triggering and gate triggering. The first three usually happen by accident, light triggering suits special high voltage valves, and gate triggering is the everyday method.

Forward voltage triggering

Anode voltage raised above the breakover voltage VBO with the gate open makes J2 avalanche and the device latch.

Best for: Explaining the VI curve; never used deliberately
Avoid
dv/dt triggering

A fast rising anode voltage charges the J2 junction capacitance, and the charging current i = C × dv/dt acts like a gate current.

Best for: Understanding false firing and snubber design
Fault
Temperature triggering

Leakage across J2 rises steeply with temperature and can fire the SCR without a gate signal.

Best for: Thermal design checks and heat sink sizing
Fault
Light triggering

Photons near J2 create electron hole pairs that act as gate current in a light activated SCR (LASCR).

Best for: HVDC valves and optically isolated firing
Special
Gate triggering

A gate to cathode current above IGT fires the SCR at the instant you choose.

Best for: Rectifiers, AC controllers, drives and chargers
Preferred
MethodTrigger sourceControlled?Typical status

Littelfuse explains in its thyristor application note that when C dv/dt becomes equal to or greater than the thyristor IGT, the device switches on. So a fast line transient can fire an SCR with no gate signal at all.

Myth: An SCR needs gate current all the time it conducts.
Fact: Once anode current passes the latching current IL, the SCR stays on even after the gate signal is removed.
Myth: Forward breakover is a valid way to fire an SCR.
Fact: Breakover is uncontrolled, stresses the junction and is avoided in real designs; it is shown on the VI curve to explain the device.
Myth: Removing the gate pulse turns the SCR off.
Fact: The gate has no turn off control; anode current must fall below the holding current IH, as it does at a natural current zero on AC.

Why Is Gate Triggering Preferred?

Gate triggering is preferred because you fire the SCR at an exact, repeatable instant with little power, while the other effects depend on line transients, heat or breakdown. Of all the SCR triggering methods, it is the one that gives you practical phase control.

Gate triggering gives you
  • Firing angle control from 0 to nearly 180 degrees
  • Low trigger power
  • Isolation through a pulse transformer or optocoupler
  • Easy synchronisation with the 50 Hz supply
Other turn on methods suffer from
  • No control over the firing instant
  • Possible damage at breakover
  • Dependence on transients and temperature
  • False firing that can short a converter leg
Quick Tip

Check the datasheet for IGT and VGT at the lowest operating temperature, not at 25 °C. Gate sensitivity falls as the junction gets colder, so a circuit that fires on the bench can fail in a cold panel.

Types of Gate Triggering: DC, AC and Pulse

Gate triggering comes in three forms: DC, AC and pulse. Among practical SCR triggering methods, pulse triggering wins because it keeps gate loss low and the control side isolated.

DC triggering drives the gate continuously from a DC source, which wastes gate power, gives no isolation and adds heating in the reverse half cycle.

AC triggering takes the gate signal from the same AC supply through a resistor or RC network, with a diode to block negative gate voltage.

Pulse triggering sends short current pulses at the chosen firing angle, so average gate power is small, and a pulse transformer or optocoupler gives the isolation needed between a low voltage controller and the 230 V power circuit.

The pulse must stay on long enough for anode current to rise past the latching current IL. With an inductive load, current rises slowly, so designers use a wider pulse or a pulse train.

Field note
The 1 k ohm gate to cathode resistor bypasses dv/dt and leakage current away from the gate. Sensitive gate SCR datasheets often state their ratings with such a resistor fitted.
Advertisement

RC Triggering Circuit of SCR

An RC triggering circuit delays the gate voltage with a capacitor charged through a variable resistor, so the SCR fires later in each half cycle. Of the simple AC SCR triggering methods, it extends the firing range beyond the 0 to 90 degree limit of resistance triggering.

Resistance triggering cannot fire later than 90 degrees because gate voltage peaks with the supply. The capacitor shifts that phase; see our page on RC and RL time constants.

Textbook design rule for half wave RC triggering
RC ≥ 1.3 × (T / 2)
50 Hz supply: T = 20 ms, so RC ≥ 13 ms
With C = 0.47 µF: R ≥ 13 ms / 0.47 µF = 27.7 k ohm

A larger R slows the charge, giving a later firing angle and a lower average load voltage.

UJT Triggering Circuit for SCR

A UJT triggering circuit uses a unijunction transistor relaxation oscillator to make sharp pulses that fire the SCR through a pulse transformer. It is the classic lab circuit for pulse based SCR triggering methods.

UJT relaxation oscillator period
T = R × C × ln[1 / (1 minus η)]
R = 10 k ohm, C = 0.1 µF, η = 0.63
T = 1 ms × 0.994 = 0.994 ms, so f ≈ 1 kHz

C charges through R to the UJT peak point voltage, then dumps through emitter and base 1 into the pulse transformer. A zener clipped supply from the same AC line resets it at each zero crossing, keeping pulses in step with the mains.

Modern boards use a firing IC, a microcontroller timer or a 555 timer instead. The idea is the same: a timed pulse after each zero crossing.

Do You Know?

The UJT standoff ratio η typically lies between about 0.5 and 0.8, so the period stays close to RC.

How to Calculate the SCR Gate Resistor

To calculate the SCR gate resistor, subtract VGT from the drive voltage and divide by the gate current you want, which is the datasheet maximum IGT times a margin factor. A margin of about 2 covers cold starts and part to part spread.

Solved example (calculator defaults)
Vg = 12 V, VGT = 1.5 V, IGT max = 30 mA, k = 2
Ig = k × IGT = 2 × 30 = 60 mA
Rg = (12 minus 1.5) / 0.060 = 175 ohm
P = 0.060² × 175 = 0.63 W for DC drive

The nearest standard E12 value is 180 ohm, which gives 10.5 / 180 = 58.3 mA, still almost twice IGT. With pulse drive, average resistor power falls by the duty cycle, but you should still check peak gate current against the datasheet IGM rating using Ohm law.

SCR Gate Resistor Calculator
Gate resistor, gate current and resistor power
Rg = 175.0 ohm | Ig = 60.0 mA | P = 0.63 W

Once the SCR conducts, on state drop times load current heats it, so size the cooling with our heat sink calculator; a hot junction can bring temperature triggering back into play.

Troubleshooting: Why an SCR Will Not Turn On

An SCR that will not turn on usually has too little gate voltage or current, a pulse too short for the load, or load current below the latching value. Work through the flowchart from the top, starting at the gate.

SymptomLikely causeFix
No firing at allGate polarity reversed or open pulse windingCheck G and K wiring, test pulse on scope
Fires warm, fails coldIGT rises at low temperatureIncrease gate current margin
Fires, drops out at oncePulse ends before IL is reachedWider pulse or pulse train
Fires without a pulsedv/dt or noise on gateAdd RC snubber and RGK resistor

False firing from line transients is the opposite problem, and the cure is an RC network across the device. Our guide on RC snubber circuit design shows how to size it, and the same physics drives the dv/dt filter used on VFD outputs.

Quick Tip

Measure gate voltage directly between gate and cathode at the device terminals with an isolated scope probe. A reading taken at the driver board misses drops in long twisted pair runs and loose connectors.

  • Gate pulse amplitude above VGT at the SCR terminals
  • Gate current at least twice the cold IGT
  • Pulse width long enough for the load to reach IL
  • Heat sink sized for full load on state loss
  • Fuse rated to protect the SCR I²t

For the fuse, our fuse selection guide explains I²t coordination. Semiconductor fuses must clear before the SCR surge rating is exceeded.

SCR Triggering Methods FAQ

What are the five SCR triggering methods used in power electronics?

The five SCR triggering methods are forward voltage, dv/dt, temperature, light and gate triggering. Gate triggering is the standard method because it sets the firing angle precisely.

The first three are faults to prevent, while light triggering suits HVDC valves.

Why is gate pulse triggering preferred over DC gate triggering for SCR?

Pulse triggering keeps average gate power low, because current flows only for tens of microseconds each cycle. It also allows isolation through a pulse transformer or optocoupler.

DC triggering heats the gate continuously and adds heating in the reverse half cycle.

How to calculate the gate resistor value for an SCR step by step?

Take the drive voltage, subtract VGT, then divide by the gate current, which is IGT times a margin of about 2. For 12 V, 1.5 V and 30 mA, Rg = 10.5 / 0.060 = 175 ohm.

Then check resistor power, here 0.63 W for DC drive, and pick the nearest standard value of 180 ohm.

What is the difference between latching current and holding current in SCR?

Latching current IL is the minimum anode current needed to keep the SCR on just after the gate pulse is removed. Holding current IH is the lower current below which a conducting SCR turns off.

IL is usually two to three times IH, so the gate pulse must last until load current crosses IL.

Why does an SCR turn on without a gate pulse in a panel?

False firing usually comes from dv/dt triggering by line transients, gate noise or high junction temperature. A fast voltage rise charges junction capacitance and the current acts like gate current.

Fit an RC snubber, a 1 k ohm gate to cathode resistor and twisted gate leads.

What We Learn Today

  • SCR triggering methods include forward voltage, dv/dt, temperature, light and gate triggering, and only gate and light triggering give a controlled firing instant.
  • Pulse gate triggering through a pulse transformer or optocoupler keeps gate loss low, isolates the controller and handles inductive loads with wider pulses or pulse trains.
  • Size the gate resistor as drive voltage minus VGT divided by twice IGT, then check resistor power, peak gate current and the cold temperature datasheet values.
